newsitem.title: USA: Georgian diplomat charged in deadly car crash. [CORRECTED 01:18 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Georgian diplomat charged in deadly car crash. [CORRECTED 01:18 GMT]

text.p: A Georgian diplomat, stripped of his diplomatic immunity, surrendered to police and was charged on Thursday with causing a five-car accident that killed a teenage girl and injured four others.
Gueorgui Makharadze, the second highest-ranking official at the Georgian embassy, told reporters after a court hearing that he wanted to express his "deepest sorrow" for "this horrible accident."

Makharadze said he prayed to God the day after the Jan. 4 accident that killed Joviane Waltrick, a 16-year-old Brazilian girl who had been living in a Maryland suburb. He acknowledged the "unspeakable loss" for her family.
He was charged with drinking and speeding on the night of the accident and faces criminal charges that carry up to 70 years in prison.

Georgian President Eduard Shevardnadze (corrects spelling of the surname from 'Schveradnadze') last weekend made the rare decision to waive diplomatic immunity in the case. Makharadze, who had been a rising star in the Georgian foreign service, said he would respect his nation's decision.
He noted that defendants under the American legal system are presumed innocent, and urged that people "wait until all the facts are known" before making any judgments.
Makharadze initially was arrested and charged with involuntary manslaughter and four counts of aggravated assault.

At a brief court hearing, he surrendered his passport and was released to the custody of a Georgian embassy official. He must report to authorities once a week and his next court appearance has been set for March 4.

At an earlier news conference announcing the charges, U.S. Attorney Eric Holder said blood tests taken two hours after the accident at a hospital showed Makharadze had an alcohol level almost twice the legal limit.
He said witnesses said he had been driving as fast as 80 miles per hour (129 kph), right before the crash.

In an affidavit with the arrest warrant, police detective Michael Harvey said Makharadze "operated his vehicle while intoxicated at a grossly excessive speed and in a reckless manner in an area congested with pedestrians and traffic."
He said several witnesses testified that Makharadze, right before the crash, was among a party of three that had dinner at a restaurant, and that they drank three carafes of wine.
Harvey said the witnesses said that Makharadze also had several other glasses of wine and a shot of liqueur.
Harvey recounted witness testimony that Makharadze had been "dodging in and out of traffic" to pass other cars and had been travelling three times the speed limit on the downtown street.

The witnesses say Makaradze lost control of his car and ran into a vehicle waiting at a stop light, Harvey said. The force of the crash catapulted the second vehicle into a third car, killing Waltrick, who was a passenger in it.

The day after the accident, Makharadze said during a police interview that he drank only two glasses of wine and that the regular and emergency brakes on his 1997 model Ford Taurus car had failed. He said the gas pedal had stuck.
But Harvey said a city mechanic and two outside experts inspected the car after the crash and concluded the brakes and the accelerator pedal had not failed.
E. Lawrence Barcella and Kirby Behre, two defence attorneys for Makharadze, said Harvey's account was "one-sided and contains numerous inaccuracies and material omissions."

They said "this slanted story ... only serves to further reduce the chances that Mr. Makharadze will receive a fair trial." They said the charges were far more severe than usual in such cases, which was denied by the prosecutors.
